title: Criminal Records: No Thanks!
summary: Josh and Chuck explain criminal records in the United States: what a criminal record contains, how records are stored across local, state and federal databases, and how expungement and sealing work. They cover juvenile records being sealed at eighteen, sex offender registry and recidivism, employer background checks and "ban the box" laws, and fidelity bonding. They then discuss research on when a former offender stops being statistically distinguishable from the general public (desistance), mass incarceration and racial disparities, and economic costs of barring people with records from work. The episode closes with listener mail about MRI physics from a radiographer in Sydney, Australia. The hosts note this episode updates their 2012 episode "Why You Probably Have a Criminal Record."

entities.name: Center for Economic Policy and Research
Why You Probably Have a Criminal Record

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to criminal records
segments.summary: The hosts joke about cameras and cussing, then introduce the topic, noting they covered it in 2012 and that about one in three or one in four Americans have a criminal record. They define a criminal record and mention mug shots.

segments.title: Expungement and sealing of records
segments.summary: The hosts explain that records are not destroyed by default. Expungement can destroy a case file, while sealing keeps records that are accessible only by court order. Traffic violations are generally not part of a criminal record, though some serious driving offenses appear on the National Driver Register.

segments.title: Juvenile records and sex offender registry
segments.summary: Juvenile records are typically sealed at eighteen if the offense was minor or non-violent and the youth stayed clean. Juveniles convicted of sex offenses can end up on the sex offender registry. Sex offenders have high recidivism rates.

segments.title: How criminal records are stored and shared
segments.summary: Records historically sat in local police stations. Today they live in state and local databases, with some uploaded to state repositories and the FBI's Interstate Identification Index, and uploading is not uniformly required. Only law enforcement and courts can access the federal index; states decide public access.

segments.title: Employer background checks and disclosure
segments.summary: Many employers run background checks and need applicant permission. Applicants should be honest about records, since lying can get them rejected. Employers may ask whether applicants were arrested versus convicted. Some employers say they would move on after a record, though many would not disqualify the candidate.

segments.title: Discrimination, housing, and fidelity bonding
segments.summary: People with arrest or conviction records can be refused jobs and public housing. Some felony drug convictions are protected from discrimination in certain cases. Fidelity bonding, often provided free by the federal government, insures employers against losses caused by hiring workers with records.

segments.title: Pros and cons, and desistance research
segments.summary: Criminal records support recidivism research. Researchers Alfred Blumstein and Kiminori Nakamura studied about 88,000 New York State records over 25 years and found that people with a serious first offense became statistically no more likely than the general public to be arrested after about eight years, and about three years for less serious crimes.

segments.title: Mass incarceration, racial disparities, and economic costs
segments.summary: The hosts discuss roughly 2.2 million people incarcerated in the US, with incarceration rising sharply from the 1980s. Black men are about six times and Hispanic men about two and a half times more likely than white men to be incarcerated. Unemployment after release and lost economic output from exclusion from work are discussed, citing a Center for Economic Policy and Research study.

segments.title: Ban the box, licensing, and reform ideas
segments.summary: Reform ideas include automatic sealing after a period of clean record, ban the box or fair chance laws limiting when employers can ask about records, and time limits on background digs. Exceptions exist for jobs involving vulnerable populations. Occupational licenses such as barbering often bar people with records.

segments.title: Listener mail: MRI follow-up from a radiographer
segments.summary: A listener from Sydney, Australia, Russell, who works as an MRI radiographer, praises the show's MRI episode and adds that lower-strength magnets need longer scan times, that three Tesla is the highest strength widely used clinically, that seven Tesla machines are FDA-approved for clinical use, and that higher research magnets have interesting effects.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and give the email address for listener mail.
